generatedProse.concept-context: In the School of Sport, integrating sources means using them to support your argument, not reporting them one after another. In sport coaching and physical education, those sources might be coaching studies, a session-plan review and a governing-body guideline. The weaker habit lists what each one found, so the paragraph reads as a summary of the reading. The stronger habit puts your point first and brings sources in to back it, qualify it, or set up a contrast. The voices technique keeps your own voice in charge: you state the point, bring in supporting and contrasting sources, then close with your own judgement.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two sport coaching students writing a paragraph that draws on the same four sources.

Tom writes: one study found the drill improved passing; another reported the same; a third noted a different pattern in young players; a fourth found the gain had faded by season's end. Each sentence reports a source, in the order he read them. The paragraph is accurate, but it has no point of its own. The reader learns what four authors found, not what Tom makes of it. This is reporting.

Amara opens in her own voice with the paragraph's point about when the drill helps, then brings the sources in to serve it: a supporting study, a second that reinforces it, then a contrasting study that complicates the picture for young players. She closes in her own voice with a short judgement that weighs them. The same four sources now support an argument. This is the voices technique.

Both students used the sources. Only Amara kept her own voice in charge of the paragraph.
generatedProse.summary: In the School of Sport, integrating sources means using them to support your argument rather than reporting them. The voices technique keeps your own voice in charge: you state the point, bring in supporting and contrasting sources, then close with a judgement. This holds whether the sources are coaching studies, lab trials or policy reports. You can now tell using a source from reporting it, and arrange several voices in a single paragraph. The next lesson sharpens this into a critical edge.

check.body: In the worked example, how did Amara weave the four sources into one paragraph?

items.text: Her own voice first, then supporting and contrasting sources, then a closing judgement.
By reporting each source in turn in the order she read them.
By removing the contrasting study so her point looked stronger.
By quoting all four sources at length with no comment.

feedback.correct: That's right. Amara led in her own voice and arranged supporting and contrasting sources around it.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the option where Amara's voice frames the sources.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara opened in her own voice, brought in supporting and contrasting sources, and closed with a judgement. The others report, cut or quote.
